https://www.dw.com/en/myanmar-aung-san-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IAOK An image released by Myanmar's junta appears to show Aung San Suu Kyi shaking hands with a Red Cross representative Image: picture alliance/dpa/Myanmar President Office via AP Advertisement Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, marking one of the only publicly confirmed contacts between the 81-year-old Nobel laureate and an outside party since the military ousted her government in February 2021. The meeting, held in the capital Naypyitaw with ICRC resident representative Arnaud de Baecque, was announced by Myanmar's military-backed government, which released four photographs of the encounter. What do we know about the meeting? Two images show Suu Kyi shaking hands with and meeting de Baecque in a sparsely furnished room. The government did not disclose further details of what was discussed. The former leader met with an ICRC representative in Naypyidaw Image: Myanmar Government spokesperson/Handout/REUTERS Two other photos offer a rare glimpse into her circumstances: Suu Kyi is shown cutting a pink birthday cake in what appears to be her residence, with a clothes rack and storage boxes visible in the background. The cake's inscription — "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu" — suggests the images may have been taken around her 81st birthday in June. While it could not be independently verified when or where the photos were taken, AFP said AI analysis found no signs the images were fabricated. One of the images shared by Myanmar's government showcases a cake. Image: Myanmar President Office/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance When was Aung San Suu Kyi last seen in public? Suu Kyi has had no confirmed public sightings since her 2021 detention, and her exact whereabouts and details about her health have been difficult to determine. She is serving a 27-year sentence on charges her allies say were politically motivated. In late April, following elections that installed former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing as president , authorities said her sentence had been commuted by one-sixth as part of a broader prisoner amnesty and that she had been moved from prison to house arrest. Despite that shift, the new administration has largely resisted outside access to her. A May request from the Philippines, on behalf of the regional Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) bloc, to allow a special envoy to visit Suu Kyi was turned down. Pressure for access has been building from other ASEAN members as part of broader efforts to resolve Myanmar's political crisis, now compounded by a civil war that followed the coup. Suu Kyi's younger son, Kim Aris, who lives in London, has led an online campaign with Myanmar democracy activists demanding proof that his mother is alive and in good health, saying he has gone years without hearing from her. Myanmar's junta said in December that she was "in good health." The ICRC did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the meeting, according to Reuters. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP View image in fullscreen A bomb disposal robot and forensic technician at Leipzig airport on Wednesday. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP Germany Leipzig drone bomb was found near Ukrainian plane carrying ammunition, say police Germany investigating whether foreign state involved as minister says ‘ripped’ detonator stopped device going off Europe live – latest updates Deborah Cole in Berlin Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.06 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A catastrophe with multiple casualties was possibly narrowly averted by the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, German officials said, as they examined whether a foreign state could be behind the plot. One of the Ukrainian aircraft next to where the bomb drone was found was loaded with military ammunition, according to a classified police report quoted by the public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the Süddeutsche newspaper. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, who said on Wednesday Germany faced a “new level of danger” , said only an apparently “ripped” detonator had prevented the device going off near Ukrainian cargo planes on the tarmac at the shipping and military hub. View image in fullscreen Police officers search an area at Leipzig airport after the discovery of the drone. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP The highly explosive Ukrainian cargo, with a tank filled with jet fuel, had apparently been transported from France to Leipzig shortly beforehand and was presumably intended for onward transport, the report said. The airport is about 12.5 miles (20km) from the centre of Leipzig, a city of more than 600,000 people. The facility hosts a major cargo processing centre that employs hundreds of people round the clock and is adjacent to two busy autobahn routes. The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe Read more The Bild newspaper reported that the drone found near the Ukrainian plane had a handmade remote detonator that did not work, and investigators hoped it could offer clues as to its origin and the culprits. Leipzig airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which German and European authorities say has carried out repeated sabotage attacks. The German government and authorities have stopped short of pointing the finger at Moscow for what marked a clear escalation of the threat level in Europe . But Dobrindt said investigators were treating the incident as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario” with a focus on “foreign powers” as likely perpetrators. View image in fullscreen The airport is a Nato and German military logistics hub and the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe. Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters Roderich Kiesewetter, a member of the German parliament’s intelligence committee, blamed Russia directly. “I consider the threat to Germany posed by hybrid attacks orchestrated by Russia to be serious,” said Kiesewetter, a member of the co-ruling Christian Democrats. “I also believe that the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport was a targeted hybrid attack – in other words, an attempted act of terrorism – orchestrated by Russia .” An airport staff member discovered the drone shortly before midnight on Tuesday, “hovering” near the ground between two Antonov Airlines An-124 cargo airplanes, among ​the world’s biggest freighters. Police said a drone defence sensor system at the airport, considered “critical infrastructure” by Germany, had not picked up the drone. They now believe based on security footage it had been on site for several hours before it was found. Dobrindt told reporters that the drone seemed to have been modified to circumvent electronic detection. It was attached to a package of explosives roughly the size of a fist, according to the WDR-NDR-Süddeutsche report, and investigators said the substance inside was believed to be semtex, a powerful plastic explosive. The discovery of the drone led the airport to suspend air traffic, forcing a DHL cargo plane from Marseille on its approach to take off again. It then collided with what is believed to have been a second drone. The media report said that plane had also been carrying unspecified “dangerous goods” before it made an emergency landing in Hanover, about 155 miles north-west, with minor damage. Bild said the drone that hit the DHL plane had a camera used to film the attack. Air traffic had been diverted on Wednesday from the airport’s southern runway but was back to normal on Thursday with no additional security measures reported. Ukraine has been using Leipzig airport as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records. German defence ministry officials said its armed forces were not conducting military transport operations at the airport at the time of the incident. The airport has previously been targeted. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the facility in July 2024 while a second was sent to the UK and caught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham . Two similar packages were also found in Poland. A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who were suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. Testimony this week at a trial in Lithuania of five people suspected of mailing the incendiary devices showed how narrowly the plane from Leipzig avoided being set on fire in mid-flight . A DHL company representative told the court the parcel ignited on the ground at its logistics centre at Leipzig airport shortly before loading, rather than during the flight, because the plane was delayed. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-s.text: STOCKHOLM — Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson must urgently take action to address claims that his potential far-right coalition partner may have been infiltrated by Russia ahead of this month’s general election, the front-runner in the race told POLITICO. The call by Magdalena Andersson, leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, which polls have on course to win the Sept. 13 election, comes after the campaign was rocked by claims that an official inside the far-right Sweden Democrats party had longstanding ties to Russia. If Andersson wins, she’ll join embattled Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as one of the few center-left politicians around the European leaders’ table. However, the gap between her coalition and a right-wing faction led by Kristersson has been narrowing as the election draws near. If Kristersson wins, the Sweden Democrats stand to enter government for the first time after the prime minister said he would govern with the far-right party. Advertisement Advertisement “Ulf Kristersson must come clean about the security crisis,” Andersson told POLITICO in an interview. “These are extremely serious allegations … Russia is the greatest threat to Sweden.” The claims, laid out in a Sept. 3 article by non-governmental group Expo, allege that a female Sweden Democrats official promoted pro-Kremlin narratives for a decade, cultivated ties with a Russian state-backed group in Sweden, and brought Russian family members onto the grounds of the Swedish parliament. The official, Polina Malaberg, who remains employed by the Sweden Democrats, previously held roles linked to parliamentary committees focusing on EU affairs. Reports that Hungary’s former foreign minister had spoken with Moscow during high-level EU gatherings set alarm bells ringing in Brussels about the risk of Russia eavesdropping on European affairs. Malaberg’s partner, Gustav Gellerbrant, is a senior civil servant and Sweden Democrats member who heads the party’s Coordination Office inside the government, acting as a liaison between the party and Kristersson’s current governing coalition. While Gellerbrant himself is not accused of Russia ties, his relationship with Malaberg raises questions about his security clearance, Andersson argues. “Is there information relating to national security that may have been exposed?” Andersson asked. “What measures has the prime minister taken and what measures does he intend to take?” Both Kristersson and Jimmie Åkesson, leader of the Sweden Democrats, have publicly addressed Expo’s claims. Kristersson said Malaberg should be fired if the allegations turn out to be true. “We are in a European war … You can’t have people who sit around promoting pro-Russian narratives and work in the Swedish parliament,” he told newspaper Aftonbladet . Advertisement Advertisement Åkesson said his party had been unaware of the pro-Kremlin posts by Malaberg but conceded “we have to look at this and sort this out,” adding that the party was investigating the claims and that Malaberg could not continue to work for them if she maintained her pro-Russian views. But these answers aren’t enough, said Andersson, a former finance minister and prime minister of Sweden. “When did the prime minister’s office become aware of this, and what information has been given to the prime minister?” she asked, adding: “This is about Sweden and the security of the Swedish people.” Speaking to POLITICO from her parliamentary office in Stockholm, Andersson argued that the risks of having the Sweden Democrats in government go beyond security. “We’ve seen journalists threatened” since Kristersson started ruling with backing from the Sweden Democrats, she said. “NGOs are threatened if they criticize what the government is doing. They’ve been threatened to have their state support withdrawn.” Ulf Kristersson has been in power since 2022. | Pool photo by Jaimi Joy via EFA/EPA “There could be a Swedish government where half of the ministers, including the foreign minister and the EU minister, come from a party that thinks we should have an inquiry on exit” from the European Union, she added. The question is whether Swedish voters will agree with Andersson that it’s time for a change (Kristersson has been in power since 2022). Security and migration remain top campaign issues. Kristersson’s camp vows to crack down harder on gang violence while ramping up deportations, including plans to deport some migrants who have been schooled in Sweden when they turn 18. Advertisement Advertisement Quizzed about her migration stance, Andersson said Sweden’s previously open border policy was “unsustainable.” The country now requires a “very strict” migration policy, she said, adding that her party is open to supporting third-country “return hubs” — external deportation centers for migrants whose asylum applications have failed — if she wins. But she said a Sweden Democrats proposal to strip permanent residency from some migrants crosses a line. “Once you have permanent residency, it’s permanent, right? You can’t say yes and then ‘no, we changed our minds’… That’s not how Sweden works. Many of these people work. They are bus drivers. They are entrepreneurs creating work… It’s insane.” Asked whether she was closer to Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen or Spain’s Sánchez on migration, Andersson sidestepped, citing both as close contacts in Europe’s center-left camp. Andersson touted strong support for Ukraine, a continued “frugal” stance on EU budget negotiations, and tough-on-crime policies as areas where she would maintain continuity with Kristersson’s government. She also favored using Russia’s frozen assets to help fund Ukraine and opposed “decoupling” with the United States. “Many people say it’s enough now” with Sweden’s current government, Andersson concluded. “We’re the Social Democratic Party. Jobs and household economy, together with welfare, schools, hospitals and elderly care. These are the main issues.”

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Stéphane Blais SEB Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save RIGA - On a Thursday morning in August, about 20 executives from Latvia's largest companies gathered in a former plywood factory. The business leaders were not there to discuss market opportunities of market growth. Instead, they learned how to fly drones and familiarize themselves with the latest technology redefining modern warfare. The old factory, in Latvia's capital city of Riga, is now known as the Drone House. It provides a glimpse into local efforts by citizens organizing to strengthen their defences against growing threats from Russia in the context of a NATO mission that is led by Canada. Local residents are learning how to fly and operate drones at the centre, which includes a 2,500-square-metre indoor hall and a 10,000-square-metere outdoor training area. While taking a break from the training, businesswoman Laura Pica said she believes Latvians have a responsibility to defend their country. "Look what we see in Ukraine, if civil citizens would not help, then probably Ukraine would be occupied," she told The Canadian Press inside the training centre. "This is why we need to help our country to strengthen their forces." Being Russia's neighbour is like standing next to "a monkey juggling with grenades," she said. "You can never know when it falls down," she added. Pica's concerns are widespread in the Baltic country. NATO shot down a drone loaded with explosives in eastern Latvia three days prior. Latvian authorities believe the drone was a Ukrainian aircraft that got diverted into Latvian airspace by Russian jamming. “(Russia is) testing our limits and NATO limits,” said Maris Bruza, one of the four founders of the Drone House. Testing those limits could include an operation to seize a portion of Latvian territory, just to see how NATO will react, he added. The ambitious civilian project aims to train 50,000 citizens in the use of drones, including high school students who receive free training. Even Ukrainian soldiers made their way to Drone House to provide training on the use of interceptor drones. The machines are designed to detect, track and neutralize enemy drones. “At the moment, Ukrainians are the best in the world," said Viesturs Silenieks, a co-founder of the Drone House. "No doubt that the best knowledge, expertise and practice comes from Ukraine." He explained that members of his team regularly travel to Ukraine, while Ukrainian military personnel frequently visit the Drone House to train and exchange information on the latest technologies developed on the front lines. Among those training at the Drone House was Daiga Auzina, who has worked as a financial services manager for 20 years. While she joked she does not have the skills to be a drone pilot, she stressed that investing in security and defence is crucial for Latvians. "It's on everybody's mind today, it is our reality," she said. "It's not realistic to expect that governments will be able to help and cover every area." Auzina became emotional talking about the presence of Canadian soldiers, who have crossed the ocean to provide military support. "I'm crying now because I think it's just so great that Canadians are helping us," she said. Canada is leading a mission to "reassure, deter and defend" the Baltic states. But the situation is becoming increasingly complex. With cyberattacks, armed drones, infrastructure sabotage, and disinformation campaigns, Latvia is facing threats that blur the line between war and peace. Latvia's new defence minister, Raivis Melnis, was appointed last May during a political crisis triggered by repeated drone attacks. The crisis led to the resignation of former prime minister Evika Silina. Melnis, a former military officer, told The Canadian Press that Latvia is taking a proactive approach to the conflict that involves younger generations. For example, the country reinstated conscription and added a mandatory national defence education course to school curriculums in 2024. The 112-hour course, spread over two years, allows students to develop military skills and includes drone pilot training, according to the minister. In Murjani, about 50 kilometres from Riga, volunteers aged 16 to 20 are preparing to participate in a drone-piloting competition using machines they assembled themselves. The competition is the culmination of a two-week camp attended by members of the “Jaunsardzes,” the youth national guard. Alesa Maza, 16, said it's important to educate young people about drones “to demystify their intimidating aspect” and prevent panic when, for example, a drone enters the country’s airspace. She said students are learning about the size of drones, their capabilities, what the aircraft can achieve and what to do when a drone is shot down. After all, the teenager lucidly explained, drones are becoming an increasingly common part of Latvians' lives, and “we're going to be seeing them more so it's just good to understand what it actually is.” For many Latvians, defence is no longer just a matter for the military — it is everyone’s responsibility. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2026. --- This report was produced with a grant from the Fonds québécois en journalisme international.
